# Why Draupnir is spelled that way — and what it costs to get it right

There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *draupnir*. This is the file on how **Draupnir** replaced it.

Draupnir's dossier divides cleanly in two: Skáldskaparmál tells its making, in the wager that also produced Gullinbursti and Mjǫllnir, and the Baldr cycle tells its journey — into the fire with the dead god and back out of Hel with the living one's token. Between those poles the Poetic Edda catches it twice: offered and refused in Skírnismál, and catalogued as a dwarf's own name in Völuspá.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Draupnir
- **ASCII form:** draupnir
- **Meaning:** "The dripper"
- **Domain of influence:** Odin's Ring, Wealth
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Classification:** Tier 2
- **Original script:** ᛏᚱᛅᚢᛒᚾᛁᚱ
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 101 of 397

## The Name Before the Marks


Spoken, the name runs `/ˈdrɑup.nir/` — 'DROYP-nir' — two syllables, stress on the first; 'droyp' rhyming with 'cowp', the au a single gliding vowel, the r's trilled.

## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Draupnir** lives at [/sites/draupnir/](/sites/draupnir/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/draupnir/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/draupnir/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/draupnir/patterns/).

The restoration keeps one feature the ASCII form drops. One is enough to matter, and the label says so plainly: Tier-2.

## Where the Name Stood First

Draupnir is a literary object: no inscription names it, and no find can be identified with it — but the ring it describes belonged to one of the best-attested object-classes in the northern record. Gold and silver arm-rings are the standard currency of Viking-Age hoards: the great Gotlandic deposits, crowned by the Spillings hoard of 1999 (the largest Viking silver hoard yet found), are full of ring-money cut and weighed as bullion, the archaeological reality behind the poetry's ring-giver. The ring's social weight is documented from both sides of the conversion: Eyrbyggja saga (ch. 4) describes a twenty-ounce ring lying on the altar of the hof at Þórsnes, on which all oaths were sworn, and the Forsa ring of Hälsingland — an iron oath-ring bearing a runic law inscription, the oldest legal text in Scandinavia — survives as the practice's one famous material witness. Earlier still, the ring-swords of the Vendel-period elite, with a ring mounted on the pommel as the sign of the oath between lord and man (attested at Valsgärde and famously at Sutton Hoo), show the ring as the badge of the gift-bond itself. The manuscript witnesses are the usual two codices: Skáldskaparmál and Gylfaginning in the Codex Regius of the Prose Edda (GKS 2367 4to, c. 1300–1350), Skírnismál and Völuspá in the Codex Regius of the Poetic Edda (GKS 2365 4to, c. 1270). The temple on the web is the newest of these addresses — the first one that fits in a pocket.

## The Archetype at Work

The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) seats this temple in **3 industries**, each match argued and weighted: **Finance, Wealth & Commerce** (the dripper of wealth — eight new rings every ninth night, increase by nature rather than conquest.); **Gems, Jewelry & Luxury Materials** (odins ring — the most famous jewel of the northern treasury.); **Manufacturing, Craft & Automation** (forged by Brokkr and Sindri as one of the three masterworks — divine manufacture.). The [Resonance File](/sites/draupnir/blog/resonance/) reads those seats through the myths themselves.

## In the Sacred Texts

The Norse tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Poetic Edda](/texts/poetic-edda/) and [Prose Edda](/texts/prose-edda/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
